content: ZBP1, also referred to as Z-DNA-binding protein 1, DNA-dependent activator of IFN-regulatory factors (DAI), or DLM-1, is a protein encoded by the ZBP1 gene in humans. This protein is distinct from the nucleic acid sensor ZBP1. In other species, such as chickens or rats, ZBP1 is an abbreviation for β-actin zipcode-binding protein 1, which is homologous to the human insulin-like growth factor 2 mRNA-binding protein 1 (IMP-1) and the murine CRD-BP. These proteins are involved in mRNA transport and are classified as RNA-binding proteins (RBPs). The DLM1 gene encodes a Z-DNA-binding protein. The formation of Z-DNA is a dynamic process that is primarily regulated by the degree of DNA supercoiling. ZBP1 functions as part of an antiviral defense mechanism by recognizing DNA in the cytoplasm. During the life cycle of many viruses, there are stages where viral DNA becomes exposed in the cytoplasm. Since DNA is typically confined to the nucleus in healthy cells, the presence of DNA in the cytoplasm serves as a signal of viral infection. Proteins like ZBP1 detect this abnormality and act as indicators of infection. Upon activation, ZBP1 enhances the production of antiviral cytokines, such as interferon-beta. DLM1 binds to cytosolic viral DNA through two Z-DNA-binding domains, Zα and Zβ, located at its N-terminus, as well as a DNA-binding domain (D3). However, the role of ZBP1 in DNA sensing has been debated. It has been shown to detect Influenza A Virus (IAV) infection and trigger cell death. Since DNA is not synthesized at any stage of the IAV life cycle, it is unlikely that DNA sensing is directly involved in this context. A subsequent study revealed that ZBP1 senses the ribonucleoprotein complex of IAV to induce cell death. More recent research has identified the transcription factor IRF1 as an upstream regulator of ZBP1 expression. Additionally, zipcode-binding protein 1 (ZBP1) has been demonstrated to regulate dendritogenesis, the formation of dendrites, in hippocampal neurons.
